title: leyline-sign in cloister has drifted from LLO canonical since v0.5.0
description:
## Symptom

`cloister/rs/crates/sign/src/` is a hard fork of `ley-line-open/rs/ll-open/sign/src/` (the canonical leyline-sign per the lift commit `ley-line/3d805a6`, 2026-05-09). ll uses a symlink and stays in sync; cloister has diverged.

## Concrete diff (2026-06-24, post-LLO-v0.5.0)

Files only in cloister:
- `src/bin/` (the `leyline-sign-helper` binary, ADR-0019)
- `src/host/` (axum/hyper server + keyring client under `feature = "host"`)
- `src/cert_chain.rs`

Files in BOTH but diverged from LLO canonical:
- `src/cert.rs`, `src/cms.rs`, `src/error.rs`, `src/ffi.rs`, `src/lib.rs`, `src/oid.rs`

## Why it happened

ADR-0019 (Accepted 2026-05-12) said "extend cloister/rs/crates/sign/ with a `[[bin]]` entry for the helper". But the leyline-sign lift to LLO was 2026-05-09 — three days BEFORE the ADR was accepted. The ADR didn't account for the new canonical home. Cloister has been drifting from LLO ever since.

A prior bead `cloister-bd8c41` (closed 2026-05-10) tracked the initial sync to ll-open 0.2.0. The sync was either incomplete at the time or re-diverged with subsequent host-side work.

## Proposed fix

Two options, picking one:

**(A)** Lift cloister's host extras (`bin/`, `host/`, `cert_chain.rs`) INTO LLO under `[features] host = []`, wasm-gated so workerd builds stay byte-identical. Then cloister symlinks to LLO (matching ll's pattern). One canonical crate, three consumer configs (wasm-verifier, host-helper, both). Linked ll-open bead.

**(B)** Cloister keeps a SEPARATE `cloister-sign-host` crate that depends on `leyline-sign` from LLO (path dep → eventually published crate). cloister/rs/crates/sign/ symlinks to LLO and stays verifier-only.

(A) is cleaner if LLO accepts the AGPL-3.0+ host code; (B) is cleaner if LLO wants to keep its license boundary unambiguous (LLO is mixed; cloister is AGPL-3.0+).

## Acceptance criteria

- cloister/rs/crates/sign/src is no longer a fork of LLO canonical
- Either symlink (A) or dep relationship (B) is in place
- ADR-0019 amended with the chosen fix
- `leyline-sign.wasm` artifact stays byte-identical pre/post fix (per ADR-0019's `cloister-2a0faa` invariant)

## Related

- Prior: `cloister-bd8c41` (closed; initial ll-open 0.2.0 sync)
- ADR-0019 (sign-only helper protocol) — needs amendment
- LLO canonical: `rs/ll-open/sign/Cargo.toml` v0.5.0
- Companion LLO bead: evaluate `[features] host` (option A enabling)

title: Carry MCP readOnly annotations through resolve-inputs — a wide-surface provider is currently an all-or-nothing grant
description: Surfaced by examining lectio as a WIDE-SURFACE tool. cloister's group model carries only name + advertisedPrefix + upstreamNames, and generated_backends carry only claims/handlesPrefix/etc. There is NO readOnly, readOnlyHint, or tool-annotation field anywhere in manifest/cluster.capnp, resolve-inputs.mjs, or the backend types — verified. So a provider collapses to an all-or-nothing grant. Concretely: lectio's server.json declares readOnly per tool (10 read: memory_search/traverse/get_content/window/timeline/list_sources/describe_schema/get_by_uri/text_search/authored_activity; 2 WRITE: memory_record, memory_link). rosary is 41 tools mixing reads (rsry_bead_search, rsry_status, rsry_list_beads) with writes (rsry_bead_create, rsry_bead_close, rsry_workspace_merge, rsry_dispatch). Declaring either as one capability grants the writes to any consumer that only needed reads — which contradicts ADR-0013 slice-grant least-privilege, the substrate's own principle. The signal is FREE: readOnly/readOnlyHint is a standard MCP tool annotation the upstream servers ALREADY declare, and cloister discards it at ingest (resolve-inputs reads groups[].upstreamNames and drops the rest). Proposal: carry the annotation through resolve-inputs into the generated backend, and let a capability be requested read-only — so a consumer can require memory-read without acquiring memory-write. This is the granularity dimension a wide-surface provider forces, and it is more immediately valuable than the code-intelligence overlap (dead surface — LLO tools are never called) or egress (cloister-1569a0), because it is a least-privilege boundary the data already supports.

comments.text: CHECKED LLO FIRST (operator direction) — and it changes the design. LLO schema-bridge ALREADY has an annotation pipeline: $Doc (-> JSON Schema description), $Optional (-> drops from required), $Default(json) (-> default), and $Op lowering to ir::OpInfo { name, input, output, errors } which the outputs/tool_defs.rs emitter consumes as "verbatim MCP tool name + the struct whose schema is the inputSchema". So the canonical place to express MCP tool metadata in this ecosystem is an schema-bridge annotation, NOT a parallel cloister invention — exactly the ADR-0035 principle. OpInfo currently has NO readOnly. IMPORTANT: there are THREE surfaces, not one. (1) third-party ingest: server.json -> resolve-inputs.mjs -> generated_backends — readOnly dropped here; this is the immediate gap and needs NO LLO change. (2) cloister own tools: hand-written zod in src/tool-schemas/*.ts -> build-tool-schemas.mjs — separate path, also no readOnly. (3) LLO first-party: capnp $Op -> OpInfo -> tool_defs.rs. Note the readonly hits in LLO zod.rs are z.array().readonly() (TS array immutability), unrelated to MCP readOnlyHint. SEQUENCING: do (1) cloister-side now, naming the field to match MCP readOnlyHint so it converges; propose adding readOnly to OpInfo in LLO afterwards so first-party capnp tools express the same thing — that is an LLO-side PR, not a unilateral cloister change. Enforcement (rejecting a write tool under a read-only grant) is a distinct second step after the annotation actually survives ingest.
comments.author: rsry-cli

comments.text: CROSS-REPO COMPANION FILED: ley-line-open-e562b4 — "mcp-tool spec cannot express per-tool readOnly — upstreamNames is a flat string list, so consumers lose least-privilege granularity". This cloister bead is BLOCKED on that one: the groups block shape is LLO-owned spec (rs/ll-core/schema-spec/mcp-tool/v1, cited at scripts/resolve-inputs.mjs:391), and per-group fields are name/advertisedPrefix/upstreamNames with upstreamNames a flat string list. Adding a readOnly field cloister-side would fork an LLO-owned contract — precisely the ADR-0035 violation class. Once the spec lands (option A additive readOnlyNames on v1, or option B tools:[{name,readOnly}] in v2 — decision is on the LLO bead), the cloister work is: carry the annotation through resolve-inputs into generated_backends, then enforce it (reject a write tool invoked under a read-only grant, fail-closed, with a denied-case test).
comments.author: rsry-cli

acceptance_criteria: Tool readOnly/readOnlyHint annotations survive resolve-inputs into the generated backend; a consumer can be granted a read-only slice of a provider; a write tool invoked under a read-only grant is REJECTED fail-closed, with a test covering the denied case.

title: LLO v0.11.3 changed generated zod: every scalar/enum/list field now carries .default() — regenerate, and confirm tsc still accepts z.ZodType<Name>
description:
Filed 2026-07-28 from LLO. Shipped in **v0.11.3** (`ley-line-open-8c00c6`,
originally filed from cloister).

## What changed

The zod emitter rendered every field as unconditionally required, contradicting
capnp's append-only guarantee — which is why appending one field broke six
cloister fixtures with `ZodError: expected "string"`. It also dropped
`$Optional` and `$Default` entirely, while `json_schema.rs` honoured both, so
one IR produced two artifacts that disagreed about which fields may be absent.

Fixed. Every capnp type with an implicit default now emits it:

    metaNamespace: z.string()               ->  z.string().default("")
    tags:          z.array(..).readonly()   ->  ....readonly().default([])
    tier:          TierSchema               ->  TierSchema.default("cluster")
    flag:          z.boolean()              ->  z.boolean().default(false)
    count:         z.number().int()         ->  z.number().int().default(0)

`$Optional` now emits `.optional()`, `$Default(json)` emits `.default(json)`.

**NOT covered: appended struct fields.** capnp reads an absent struct pointer
as an all-defaults struct, but zod's `.default(v)` does not re-parse `v`, so
`.default({})` would hand consumers a value their own TS interface forbids, and
the lazily-parsed form would not terminate for a self-referential struct.
Appending a STRUCT field remains a compatibility break. Stated in
`capnp_implicit_default` rather than left implicit.

## What you need to do

1. **Regenerate.** `cluster.zod.ts` and `identity.zod.ts` will diff — every
   scalar/enum/list field gains `.default(...)`. `cluster:zod:check-drift` will
   flag it until you do. **That diff IS the fix**, not a regression.
2. **Confirm the six fixtures now parse.** They stand in for values written
   against the older schema — exactly what ADR-0004's append-only rule promises.

## The open question only you can answer

`.default()` changes zod's **input** type. The emitter declares
`export const XSchema: z.ZodType<X> = z.lazy(...)`. In zod 4 that generic's
Input parameter defaults to `unknown`, so a schema with optional inputs should
still be assignable — but **LLO runs no `tsc` and I could not verify it.**

If your typecheck rejects the regenerated output, that is an LLO bug and I will
fix it same-day; the annotation likely needs widening. Please report either way
— a confirmation is as useful as a failure, because right now nobody has
checked.

This gap is structural, not an oversight: LLO owns the generator and cannot
observe emitted-TypeScript behaviour. LLO-side coverage is property tests over
arbitrary IR asserting the emitted text accepts absence wherever capnp permits
it, mutation-verified. That checks the text; only your `tsc` checks the
semantics.

## Separately — a fail-open path in build-manifest.mjs

While mapping what could move to LLO I read `backendFromGeneratedRow`
(`scripts/build-manifest.mjs:534`). It **fails open** three ways:

    if (!row || typeof row !== "object") { console.error("skipping malformed…"); return null; }
    if (typeof row.name !== "string" || row.name === "") { console.error("skipping…"); return null; }
    const handlesPrefix = typeof row.handlesPrefix === "string" ? row.handlesPrefix : "";

A malformed `cluster.lock.toml` row is skipped, logged to stderr, and the build
SUCCEEDS — so the generated manifest silently omits a backend. A wrong-typed
`handlesPrefix` becomes `""`, which matches nothing. That is the exact inverse
of schema-bridge's `UnmappedConstruct` discipline, applied to schema-bridge's
own output.

Root cause is that the lockfile row shape is **nowhere declared**, so the author
had no schema to validate against and could only coerce. Declaring it and
generating the validator with the zod emitter you already consume would make the
fail-open path unrepresentable rather than merely fixed. Worth more than moving
any generator.

## Also: do not bump the LLO pin yet

`[inputs.llo]` is pinned at `@f62a5430` / 0.8.0. `ley-line-open-e44960` (image
publish + provenance attestation) merged in LLO but the image does not exist
until the next `v*` tag. Until then a bump gets
"could not resolve an OCI digest — pinning by MUTABLE TAG" rather than a
resolved digest. I will report when the image is live.

comments.text:
## RESOLVED before you had to look — the assignability question is answered

vigil's review made the right criticism of this bead: LLO shipped a change whose
effect it structurally cannot observe, then proposed *telling* you about the
unobserved effect rather than observing it. Fixed. Verified against zod **4.4.3**
and the `tsc` in this repo's `node_modules`, from an isolated scratch dir — no
checkout, no regeneration, nothing written to this tree (`feat/llo-11-3-pin` is
checked out and someone is working on it).

Compiled the exact shape the emitter now produces:

    export const SSchema: z.ZodType<S> = z.lazy(() =>
      z.object({
        name:  z.string().default(""),
        loud:  z.boolean().default(false),
        count: z.number().int().default(0),
        tags:  z.array(z.string()).readonly().default([]),
        tier:  TierSchema.default("cluster"),
        other: OtherSchema,          // struct ref — deliberately NOT defaulted
      }).strict());

    const parsed: S = SSchema.parse({ other: { note: "x" } });

**Result: exit 0, zero diagnostics.** Control with a deliberate type error
(`const parsed: number = …`) exits 2 with `TS2322`, so the harness bites rather
than silently passing.

Three things that establishes:

1. **`.default()` does NOT break `z.ZodType<Name>`.** zod 4 defaults that
   generic's Input parameter to `unknown`, so widened inputs stay assignable.
2. **The output type is preserved** — the control's error reads *"Type 'S' is
   not assignable to type 'number'"*, i.e. `parse()` still returns `S`. Your
   `Cluster` / `Gateway` consumers see no type change.
3. **The append-only property holds at the type level**, not just in LLO's
   text assertions: parsing a value with every defaulted field absent
   typechecks and yields `S`.

So regeneration should be a clean diff. If your `tsc` disagrees on the real
`cluster.zod.ts`, that is new information and I will fix it same-day — but the
mechanism I was worried about is not a problem.

## Correction to this bead: nothing will flag a stale cluster.zod.ts

I wrote that `cluster:zod:check-drift` would flag the drift. **Wrong**, and the
truth is worse. `generated-drift.yml` regenerates only via `task manifest` and
`task cluster:toml`, then diffs `src/generated/` — `cluster.zod.ts` is never
regenerated by that job, so a stale copy matches itself and passes. And
`cluster:zod` appears in **no workflow at all**; the task says of itself *"NOT a
verify gate yet; run manually after cluster.capnp schema edits."*

So this will not block anyone. It will sit silently wrong until someone
regenerates by hand — which is a weaker safety net than I claimed and a
stronger reason to regenerate deliberately rather than wait for CI to complain.

Credit to vigil for both corrections.

title: [design] cloister↔LLO boundary: cloister has bridge crates; leyline-* names belong in LLO
description:
## Companion to LLO design bead

This is the cloister-side of a cross-repo design thread. See LLO bead for the principle statement; this bead captures the cloister-side audit and migration.

## Strategic question (cloister perspective)

Cloister is the **agent-execution + network-topology** layer:
- workerd / Cloudflare Workers runtime
- Durable Objects (BeadStore, TrustStore, BlobStore, CredentialVault)
- Vault slice grants per ADR-0010/0013
- Bundle hypervisor, manifest enforcement
- Agent dispatch surface

What cloister should NOT be: the home for `leyline-*` primitives. The pattern that works (`cloister-cas` consuming `leyline-cas-ffi`) is **thin cloister bridge crates depending on LLO primitives**.

## Proposed principle

> Anything in cloister named `leyline-*` is a smell. It should either be:
> - **Renamed** to `cloister-*` if it's cloister-specific runtime code wrapping an LLO primitive
> - **Moved** to LLO if it's a primitive that doesn't need cloister context

## Current violations (initial audit)

- **`cloister/rs/crates/sign/` (`leyline-sign`)** — hard fork of LLO canonical. Should split:
  - LLO keeps `leyline-sign` (verifier + signer library, URI-scheme-agnostic, gated `feature = "host"` for the signing side)
  - Cloister has new `cloister-sign-host` crate (daemon binary, `keychain://com.cloister/master-sk` URI validators, axum/hyper wire, rate limiter, supervisor)
  - cloister/rs/crates/sign/src/ symlinks to LLO canonical (matches ll's pattern)
  - ADR-0019 amended

## Migration approach

1. Resolve `cloister-59c60e` (instance fix for leyline-sign) per the principle in this design thread.
2. Audit cloister for any other `leyline-*` names. Currently known:
   - `rs/crates/sign/` (this thread)
   - `dist/*-leyline_sign.wasm` (artifact name follows crate name — auto-fixes when crate renames)
3. Document the principle in cloister docs (probably as an ADR cross-linked to the LLO design doc).

## Out of scope (for this design bead)

- Specific leyline-sign fix (in `cloister-59c60e`).
- workerd/wasm component model questions (different concern).

## Acceptance criteria

- Cloister ADR documenting the principle and audit.
- All identified violations have remediation beads filed.
- Cross-repo thread closed by alignment with LLO.

## Cross-repo thread

Companion bead in LLO: filed alongside this one. Resolution requires alignment in both repos.

## Related

- `cloister-59c60e` (instance: leyline-sign drift)
- `ley-line-open-5a06e9` (instance: LLO host-feature evaluation)
- LLO design companion (filed simultaneously — id TBD)
- `cloister-bd8c41` (prior closed sync attempt)
- ADR-0019 (sign-only helper protocol)

title: Make cluster:dev a repeatable live ART-stack launch, not a dry-run-only plan
description: Live pitch-readiness probe on 2026-07-26 exposed three operator failures. First, plain `task cluster:dev` was considered up-to-date and performed no launch; `--force` was required for a side-effecting long-running task. Second, an already-running Mache on declared port 7532 was not preflighted or adopted, so the spawned bundle exited with EADDRINUSE. Third, notme reused incompatible persisted Wrangler Durable Object state and failed with `_cf_ALARM has 3 columns but 2 values were supplied`, causing the hypervisor fail-closed policy to tear down the cluster without an actionable safe-state migration/backup hint. Make the launcher uncacheable/always-run, preflight declared listeners with explicit adopt-or-refuse behavior, and give each sibling workerd bundle an explicit cluster-scoped persistence directory or a fail-safe diagnostic/remediation path. Do not silently delete persisted state. This is a launch-readiness blocker for demonstrating Cloister as the single ART MCP face.
acceptance_criteria: A repeat invocation of `task cluster:dev` actually launches without `--force`; automated launcher coverage exercises an occupied optional-service port and incompatible persisted workerd state, producing deterministic adopt/refuse and backup-safe remediation behavior; with clean declared state, health and `/mcp` tool listing succeed for the ART topology.

title: pre-push hook symlinks the pnpm launcher, breaking shim-style installs
description:
find_matching_pnpm() locates a pnpm on PATH, then exposes it via `ln -s "$PNPM_BIN" "$PNPM_SHIM_DIR/pnpm"`. The standalone pnpm launcher (~/Library/pnpm/pnpm) is a 442-byte sh script that locates its payload with `basedir=$(dirname "$0")` and execs "$basedir/.tools/pnpm/<ver>/node_modules/pnpm/bin/pnpm.mjs". Through a symlink into a temp dir, $basedir becomes the temp dir, the .tools path does not exist, and the launcher dies in Node before printing a version.

The hook then reports the empty version as:
  pre-push: expected pnpm@10.30.3 after activation, got pnpm
...and refuses to push. Reproduced on macOS with pnpm installed at ~/Library/pnpm (PNPM_HOME standalone install).

Two contributing facts worth recording:
1. The ambient pnpm here is 11.17.0, but pnpm >= 10 reads package.json#packageManager and transparently delegates, so `pnpm --version` returns 10.30.3 INSIDE the repo and 11.17.0 outside it. The pin is already honored by pnpm itself; the hook`s PATH-scan is a fragile reimplementation of that.
2. The hook comment justified the check with "pnpm 11 no longer honors this package.json`s pnpm overrides" — but package.json has no `pnpm` block at all, so that rationale is stale.

Fix: generate a wrapper that execs $PNPM_BIN by ABSOLUTE path instead of symlinking, which keeps $0 pointing at the real install while still exposing only pnpm (not the whole install dir) on PATH. Retarget the git-hooks test at that intent + add a regression guard against reintroducing `ln -s`.

comments.text:
CI caught a real gap that no local run could: ubuntu lint failed with "not ok 71 - runtime storage init dispatches to a non-mutating preview" while every macOS run was green. Fixed in 1dcd482.

The guard was already correct — sparsebundles are APFS/hdiutil, so `cloister runtime storage init` refuses off macOS with exit 2. The TEST was wrong: it asserted status === 0 plus the plan text unconditionally, so it could only ever pass on darwin.

Root cause is a testability gap rather than a bad assertion. main() read process.platform directly, so the refusal branch was unreachable on macOS dev machines and the plan branch unreachable on Linux CI. Each host silently covered whichever half it happened to be — the contract test was half-vacuous on BOTH platforms, and no local run of any kind could have caught it.

Fix threads `platform` through the existing io injection seam (alongside log/error/input/output) and unit-tests both branches, so either host now exercises both. With the seam in place the Linux failure reproduces on macOS, which is how it was finally diagnosed. The integration test now asserts the branch its host actually takes instead of skipping off macOS — asserting nothing on Linux is exactly what let the original slip through.

Diagnosis path worth recording, since four plausible causes were ruled out first, each with a real run: Task content-hash cache masking it (task lint --force + fresh node_modules — passed 1410/1410); Node version, CI being 20 vs local 25 (reproduced CI exactly via fnm 20.20.2 + corepack pnpm 10.30.3 — passed); missing .env.local in CI (moved aside, re-ran — passed); macOS-only code paths unguarded (init-krun-storage.mjs:112 already guarded). Ubuntu-vs-macOS was the only difference left, which pointed at the platform branch.

One false lead: an early Node 20 attempt appeared to reproduce a lint:shim failure, but that was an artifact — the local pnpm is the 11.17.0 shim which itself requires Node >= 22.13 and dies on node:sqlite. CI corepack pnpm 10.30.3 supports Node 20 fine.

Verified: task lint exit 0; script suite 457/457, 0 skipped (up from 455 by the two new branch tests).

title: Make nono isolation gate outer-sandbox aware
description: `task lint` under a managed Codex workspace reaches tools/harness-sandbox/test/nono-isolation.test.mjs, but the outer sandbox denies creating the deliberate `$HOME/.nono-isolation-decoy-*` fixture before nono runs. Result: 447/448 script tests pass and the file aborts at module setup with EPERM. Moving the decoy to /tmp is invalid because nono default-allows /tmp, so the gate needs an explicit outer-sandbox capability/preflight or a supported fixture location that remains denied inside nono while writable by the outer harness. Do not silently skip the kernel-denial proof on ordinary hosts.

comments.text:
Fixed; PR #190 (fix/nono-outer-sandbox), commit d9865c2, based on main.

Root cause: nono-isolation.test.mjs plants the $HOME decoy at MODULE LOAD. Inside an outer sandbox $HOME is read-only, so writeFileSync throws during module evaluation and node:test reports the whole FILE as one failure — all eight isolation assertions lost. This is exactly what Codex hit (it saw 447/448 with the decoy as the sole failure).

Reproduced deterministically without needing a real outer sandbox: a directory chmod 555 (owner bits are checked first, so the owner is denied too) pointed at via $HOME, which os.homedir() honors.
  before: pass 0, skipped 0, fail 1, exit 1 — unhandled EACCES from ModuleJob.run
  after:  pass 6, skipped 2, fail 0, exit 0 — decoy test states why it stood down

Fix: catch only EACCES/EPERM/EROFS on the decoy write and convert it into a skip reason for that ONE test; any other error still throws so a genuinely broken fixture stays loud. Cleanup made conditional too — rmSync force swallows ENOENT but not the EACCES from unlinking inside an unwritable $HOME.

The anti-vacuous guard is the important part. New contract test (3 cases) pins that degrading is SCOPED: the six $HOME-independent assertions (boot, workdir read/write, --open-port, --allow-unix-socket, --block-net) must all still execute, so a future blanket skip cannot park a real nono regression behind a green gate. A third case asserts the decoy test still RUNS on a writable $HOME, so the skip stays conditional rather than quietly retiring the assertion.

Two silent traps found while writing it, both of which made the first draft vacuous and are now documented in-file:
- the suite must be spawned as a plain script, NOT `node --test`: node:test refuses to recurse and emits no results at all, so any assertion on its output passes trivially.
- NODE_TEST_CONTEXT=child-v8 is inherited by children, making them emit V8-serialized binary frames instead of the parsed summary (every count came back null).

Also: the simulated $HOME must live under the REAL home, not tmpdir — nono roots session state at $HOME/.nono, and a $HOME under /private/var collides with nono own system-read grants ("Refusing to grant /private/var ... overlaps protected nono state root"), which would break the sandbox instead of the decoy. Its .nono is pre-created writable so nono still initializes and only the decoy write is denied.

Registered in Taskfile test:lint-scripts (sources already covered tools/harness-sandbox/test/**). Verified: task lint exit 0, task pre-push exit 0, script suite 424/424 with 0 skipped. RED confirmed before GREEN.

title: Ship a second tenant (non-MCP) to load-bear ADR-0002's protocol-agnostic claim
description:
Surfaced 2026-05-10 from an outside review:

> "ADR-0002 says 'edge router, not MCP gateway' — fine, but the entire current public face is MCP/JSON-RPC. Ship one non-MCP tenant (a tiny gRPC service, a WebSocket pub/sub) and the protocol-agnostic claim becomes load-bearing instead of aspirational. Right now the route table generality is a promise."

The reviewer is right. Current public-face routes:

| Route | Protocol | Tenant kind |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /mcp` | JSON-RPC 2.0 | MCP |
| `GET /mcp` (SSE) | JSON-RPC over SSE | MCP |
| `GET /health` | Plain HTTP/JSON | Liveness |
| `GET /.well-known/interlace/index.json` | Plain HTTP/JSON | Discovery (Interlace) |
| `GET /identity/*` | Reverse proxy to notme | Identity surface |
| `GET /interlace/peers/{fp}` | JSONL stream | Disclosure (Interlace) |

The non-MCP routes are HTTP/JSON, all narrow read-side things. NONE of them prove the EdgeRoute table can hold a tenant with different semantics (push, streaming-bidi, binary, framed).

## Why this matters for OSS readiness

- The substrate ADR (0002) is more interesting than "yet another MCP gateway."
- Reviewers who see only MCP code will reasonably ask "where's the second tenant?"
- The current route table generality is a promise; a working example makes it a property.

## What to ship

ONE small non-MCP tenant. Pick the lightest path that exercises a different protocol shape:

**Option A — WebSocket pub/sub (1-2 days):**
- `GET /ws/peers/{fp}` — WebSocket upgrade
- Server pushes peer-attestation chain UPDATES as they happen (companion to the polling JSONL stream at `/interlace/peers/{fp}`)
- Different protocol shape: bidirectional streaming, framed messages, durable subscription
- New backend kind: `webSocketTenant` in the manifest (or a more generic `streamingTenant`)
- Demonstrates: EdgeRoute can hold a connection-stateful tenant

**Option B — gRPC unary (2-3 days):**
- A tiny health/probes service that mirrors the JSON `/health` over gRPC
- Different protocol shape: HTTP/2 framed binary, protobuf wire format
- New backend kind: `grpcTenant` in the manifest, with the .proto compiled to TS via a build step
- Demonstrates: the substrate doesn't assume JSON anywhere

**Option C — Server-Sent Events for a non-MCP tenant (0.5-1 day):**
- `GET /events/interlace` — SSE stream of cluster-level events (peer join, peer leave, master rotation)
- The wire is already familiar (SSE is in the MCP route today) but the CONTENT is non-JSON-RPC — pure event records
- Demonstrates: the route-handler factoring doesn't bake MCP semantics in
- Cheapest option; arguably the lightest "load-bearing" proof

**Recommend Option C as the MVP.** SSE is in the codebase already; the proof point is that the EdgeRoute table holds a non-MCP SSE tenant without any MCP-specific glue leaking through. ~50 lines of route code + a manifest entry.

## Acceptance

- The chosen tenant ships as a new EdgeRoute, declared in cluster.capnp / cloister.capnp's manifest
- A test demonstrates the tenant works end-to-end without MCP machinery touching it
- README's "What rides on top (bundles + tenants)" section gains the new tenant
- ADR-0002 amendment notes: "first working non-MCP tenant landed in cloister-XXXXXX"

## Refs

- ADR-0002 — edge router + protocol-agnostic backends
- README "What cloister is NOT" section (just added 2026-05-10)
- cloister-be0607 (the cluster substrate that makes future tenants composable)

comments.text:

```
cloister.capnp:39  /.well-known/identity-bridge → wellKnownIdentityBridge
cloister.capnp:40  /v2                          → ociRegistry
cloister.capnp:41  /.well-known/mcp-registry    → wellKnownMcpRegistry
cloister.capnp:42  /interlace/ca-bundle         → caBundle
```

ADR-0002 has TWO amendments documenting the load-bearing demonstration:

- **2026-05-11 (`cloister-c9922f`)**: "First non-MCP tenant has landed" — `WellKnownIdentityBridgeRoute`
- **2026-05-11 (`cloister-cabd57`)**: "Second non-MCP tenant has landed ... together they form the load-bearing demonstration that ADR-0002's protocol-agnostic seam holds" — `OciRegistryRoute`

Acceptance criteria from this bead, all met:
- ✅ Non-MCP tenant ships as new EdgeRoute (5 of them)
- ✅ Tests exercise them end-to-end
- ✅ README's tenants section names them (README.md:43-44, README.md:146-152)
- ✅ ADR-0002 amendment notes the landing (twice)

The reviewer who surfaced this concern can now point at three production tenants (OIDC bridge, OCI registry, MCP registry) plus two streaming tenants (disclosure JSONL, ca-bundle). The bead's Option C (SSE non-MCP) was the lightest implementable; in practice the team picked richer tenants and they landed first.

title: backendFromGeneratedRow fails open — a malformed lockfile row is skipped and the build SUCCEEDS with a backend silently missing

comments.text:
Fixed in 7df786d (PR #214).

**Report confirmed, with one correction.**

Confirmed empirically before fixing — `handlesPrefixx` (typo) and `handlesPrefix = 42` both produce output *byte-identical* to a legitimate `handlesPrefix = ""` row:

```
typo  handlesPrefixx → {"handlesPrefix":"","claims":["a"]}
wrong type (number)  → {"handlesPrefix":"","claims":["a"]}
legit empty prefix   → {"handlesPrefix":"","claims":["a"]}
claim (singular)     → {"handlesPrefix":"mache_","claims":null}
```

The ambiguity point is right and load-bearing: `stripPrefix = ""` appears in all 15 shipped rows, so empty-string cannot also be the absent/wrong-type sentinel.

**Correction: `input` is not unread.** It is read at `build-manifest.mjs:451-465` for the cross-input name-collision diagnostic and the qualified name. Had that claim been taken at face value and `input` treated as vestigial, dropping it would have broken the collision diagnostic. It is declared in the field table rather than dropped. The defect class (unknown keys silently dropped) is real; that particular example isn't.

**Shipped:**
- `GENERATED_BACKEND_FIELDS` declares the row shape (9 fields, types verified against all 15 real rows)
- unknown key → `fail()` (exit 2); present-but-wrong-type → `fail()`
- **absent still defaults** — older lockfiles predate newer fields; rewriting them is not a precondition for building
- the `if (backend === null) continue` guard is removed, not left dead — it read as "malformed rows are skipped", the behavior being removed

**Acceptance (behavioral, as specified).** The script exports nothing, so each test feeds a crafted lockfile to the real script via `CLOISTER_LOCKFILE` and asserts the exit code — stronger than exporting for a unit test. 10 tests in `scripts/test/build-manifest-row-shape.test.mjs`, registered in `test:lint-scripts`. The shipped lockfile builds **byte-identically**.

**Two process notes, both self-inflicted and both caught by controls:**

1. First attempt put `const GENERATED_BACKEND_FIELDS` below its use — TDZ, and the overlay runs at module top level. The build crashed *before writing*, so the unchanged output file made "byte-identical" look like a pass. A vacuous pass I nearly reported. Fixed by moving the declaration above the overlay section.
2. The two positive controls ("a well-formed row builds cleanly", "absent fields default") failed initially — I had overridden `CLOISTER_TOOL_SCHEMAS`, which is an *input* to this script, at an empty temp dir. Every build failed, meaning the seven negative assertions would have passed for the wrong reason. That is exactly what the positive controls exist to catch.

Re: not applying it directly — the caution was right in general, but this tree is where the change belongs and it was clean. Noted the shared-checkout hazard.

title: The 24 lint rails have no shared harness, and mache already ships one
description:
The rails have no harness, and a sibling repo already ships one we do not use.

MEASURED, on branch `integration`:

  scripts/lint-*.mjs        24 scripts, 5389 LOC
                            18/24 re-derive ROOT from fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)
                            20/24 hand-roll process.exit(1)
                            17/24 keep their own violations[] array
                            largest: lint-bundle-isolation.mjs at 1341 LOC carrying
                            14 numbered invariants — a rules engine that grew inside
                            one file
  done-rules/ + done-runner.mjs   a SECOND rule mechanism: 5 JSON rules, 177-LOC runner,
                            its own severity model (block|warn, default block)
  mache find-smells         NOT USED. No .mache.json, no smell baseline, no reference
                            to .github/actions/find-smells anywhere in cloister.

mache already ships what we hand-rolled twice: a rule engine (cmd/smell_rules.go),
USER-SUPPLIED rules via `smellRulesDir` in .mache.json (cmd/smell_rules_config_test.go),
a ratchet baseline (smell_ratchet.go), SARIF emit to code-scanning (smell_sarif.go), and
a composite action that runs the whole gate.

The sharpest evidence: scripts/lint-smell-rule-kinship.mjs is 281 LOC whose entire job is
to record how cloister's done-runner severity model differs from mache's SmellRule severity
model. We maintain a lint to track our kinship with a harness we are not using.

THE REAL CRITIQUE (user's words: "hyper specific behavior and not real tests"). Fair, and
the rails are not one thing — they are three kinds mixed together:

  (a) properties of the shipped tree      -> these ARE real tests and mostly already live
                                             in scripts/test/. Keep.
  (b) structural smells over source shape -> belong in mache's engine as external rules,
                                             with a ratchet baseline instead of pass/fail.
                                             lint:schema-claim (added 2026-08-03) is
                                             exactly this and is filed here as a data
                                             point against itself.
  (c) drift between two files             -> should be GENERATED-then-diffed, not
                                             hand-compared. cluster:emit:check-drift and
                                             cluster:go:check-drift already do it right;
                                             several others hand-compare.

The pattern to name: one incident -> one bespoke 200-LOC script. That tests the last bug,
not the invariant, and the cost compounds — every new rail re-implements walking, collecting,
reporting and exiting.

NOT PROPOSING a big-bang refactor. Suggested order:
  1. Extract the shared harness (walk / collect / report / exit) from the 24. Mechanical,
     no behavior change, shrinks every future rail.
  2. Classify each rail a/b/c. Expect a meaningful (b) set.
  3. Pilot ONE (b) rail as a mache external rule with .mache.json + baseline. If it works,
     that is the migration path and lint-smell-rule-kinship can be deleted rather than
     maintained.
  4. Only then consider adopting the find-smells action in CI.

Raised by the user 2026-08-03 while reviewing cloister PR #260 / the execution/v1 work.
Related: cloister-2fb46a (the kinship claim this bead proposes to dissolve).
acceptance_criteria: A shared rail harness exists and at least one rail is classified+migrated as a mache external rule, OR a written decision records why cloister keeps its own.

title: Harness target is hardcoded to Anthropic — make codex or claude-code a declared profile
description:
Operator correction 2026-07-27: yesterday goal was stated as "get codex in cloister mostly working", and the agent read that as a CODE task (it built the krunvm runtime, cloister-6d7af4 / cloister-4adbdc, merged in PR #189). The actual ask is narrower and different: MAKE THE TARGET CONFIGURABLE — codex or claude-code, either one.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY HARDCODED — two module constants, scripts/harness-dev.mjs:61-62:
    const SERVICE  = "anthropic";
    const UPSTREAM = "https://api.anthropic.com";
Everything else in that script (minting the dev master + cert, vaulting the key so the harness never sees it, launching the lease shim, printing the base URL) is already provider-agnostic.

WHY THE REMAINING WORK LOOKED BIGGER THAN IT IS: Codex closing note listed "mediated OpenAI credentials, restricted outbound networking, interactive lifecycle/TTY handling, narrower workspace policy" as things CODEX needs. Re-read under the configurability framing, every one of those is PER-TARGET POLICY THE HOST CURRENTLY HARDCODES. The compute substrate is already target-agnostic — the krunvm backend runs whatever digest-pinned OCI artifact the launch plan names, which is exactly why Codex proved it with Mache rather than with Codex itself. The compute is parameterised; the policy plane is not.

THIS IS THE SAME SHAPE AS cloister-f9d473 (host hardcodes a guest DO namespaces) and as ADR-0056 (a value that does not declare what it is). The host hardcoding a guest requirements is the host guessing what the guest is; a guess can only be discovered wrong at runtime.

WHAT A TARGET PROFILE MUST CARRY (from reading harness-dev.mjs):
- service name (vault credential key)
- upstream base URL
- API-key env var name: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY vs OPENAI_API_KEY
- the base-URL env var to print for the operator to export: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL vs OPENAI_BASE_URL
- egress allowlist host (pairs with the vault environment_variable networking.allowed_hosts model)
- SUPPORTED AUTH MODES — note harness-dev.mjs:64-71 has an --audit path for Claude Code Max/OAuth where there is no key to vault. That is an Anthropic-specific capability, so it is a per-target property, not a global flag. A target that lacks it must reject --audit rather than silently forwarding unauthenticated.

DELIBERATELY NOT DECIDED HERE: whether the profile lives in cluster.toml as a first-class declaration, in a target registry file, or as a bundle-contributed declaration (which would unify it with the f9d473 question). That choice is shared with f9d473 and should probably be made once, for both.

Related: ADR-0040 (harness-in-cloister control/credential/audit plane), ADR-0042 (turnkey local harness run, the ADR this script implements), ADR-0043 (delivery plane), cloister-f9d473 (same host-guesses-guest shape), cloister-75430e (host-runtime integration epic).

title: Perf numbers for the lease pipeline + disclosure endpoint
description:
Surfaced 2026-05-10 from outside review: "Perf numbers — you agreed; nothing to argue."

Cloister's docs claim things like "v8 isolate cold start ~5ms", "capnp-over-UDS faster than HTTP-over-UDS", and "the lease middleware is on every request's hot path." None of these have measured numbers in the repo. Reviewers need concrete latency/throughput data to evaluate whether the security overhead is acceptable.

## What to measure

| Surface | Metrics |
|---|---|
| **Lease middleware p50/p99 latency** | Per-step breakdown: header parse, getCABundle (cached + uncached), wasm cert verify, sig verify, scope check, seen_nonces upsert, counter UPSERT. Total wall time per authenticated request. |
| **Tools/call dispatch overhead** | Time from request arrival to backend invocation. Pre-auth-gate vs post-auth-gate comparison so the lease cost is isolatable. |
| **TrustStore DO RPC cost** | applyAttestation, upsertLeaseCounter, recordSeenNonce — each method's serialization + IPC overhead. |
| **Disclosure endpoint throughput** | tail-N rows/sec for a long peer chain; same for paginated reads with cursor. |
| **Cold-start cluster boot** | Time from container start to first successful /mcp request, broken out by bundle (router, notme, mache, rosary). |

## How to measure

- Local: `wrangler dev` + `oha` or `hey` against the running gateway.
- Use the existing fixture cert (now valid through 2049) for authenticated requests via the `signedMcpRequest` helper.
- Aggregate into a `docs/perf/2026-XX-XX-measurements.md` file with date, environment, and numbers.
- Re-run on each major release; track regression.

## What "good" looks like for OSS launch

Numbers in:
- README "Performance" section pointing at the perf doc
- ADR-0007 amendment (lease middleware is fast enough)
- ADR-0009 (the substrate portability claim is bounded by these)

## Out of scope

- Hardware benchmarks (this isn't a competitive perf claim, it's a sanity check)
- CF Workers production numbers (defer until we have production traffic)
- Comparison to alternatives (Istio, Envoy, etc.)

## Refs

- README.md performance claims (current ones are inherited from workerd's docs, not measured)
- threat-model.md §6.2 (clock-skew bound) — implies lease overhead < 60s, but we should know exactly how far under
- ADR-0009 substrate-comparison table (boot times listed are aspirational; we should measure cloister-router specifically)

comments.text:
Lease-middleware perf shipped as docs/perf/2026-05-10-lease-pipeline.md.

Key numbers from `task bench:lease` (workerd-local via vitest cloudflarePool, M3 Max):

| Step | mean (µs) |
|---|---:|
| Header parse | 6 |
| Cert chain verify (wasm32) | 90 |
| Request sig (Ed25519) | 32 |
| Cert fingerprint (sha256) | 4 |
| seen_nonces upsert (DO RPC) | 374 |
| lease_counter upsert (DO RPC) | 386 |
| Sum of step means | 898 |
| **Full pipeline p50** | **1000** |
| **Full pipeline p99** | **3000** |

Sub-µs steps (clock-skew, claims+epoch+validity, scope match) below the noise floor.

Big finding: TrustStore DO RPCs are ~85% of pipeline time. Wasm cert verify (~10%) is the expected slow crypto step. The two RPCs back-to-back are the optimization target if we want to push the gate down — coalescing them into a single `upsertLeaseAndRecordNonce` is a ~30% pipeline-level win candidate.

Methodology caveat documented in the perf doc: `performance.now()` is 1ms-quantized in workerd, so per-step numbers come from timing entire N=500 loops and dividing. Full-pipeline numbers come from N=200 individual end-to-end calls.

Remaining four surfaces filed as cloister-e4daae (dependency added). NOT closing this parent bead — open until all five surfaces have docs.

`task lint` stays green with the changes; bench is opt-in via `task bench:lease`, configured under `vitest.bench.config.ts` so the test-perf path doesn't drag the full 619-case suite.

comments.text:
Lease-middleware piece shipped (`0f9b1d2`, on main). Per-step latency writeup in `docs/perf/2026-05-10-lease-pipeline.md`. Bench harness at `test/perf/lease-pipeline.test.ts` with opt-in `task bench:lease` (excluded from the lint gate; bench results don't gate CI).

**Numbers** (workerd-local, M3 Max, vitest cloudflarePool):

| Step | mean (µs) |
|---|---:|
| Header parse | 6 |
| Clock-skew bound | <1 |
| Cert chain verify (wasm32) | 90 |
| Claims + epoch + validity | <1 |
| Request sig (Ed25519) | 32 |
| Scope match | <1 |
| Cert fingerprint (sha256) | 4 |
| seen_nonces upsert (DO RPC) | 374 |
| lease_counter upsert (DO RPC) | 386 |
| **Full pipeline p50 / p99** | **1000 / 3000** |

**Surprise**: DO RPCs dominate at ~85% (760µs of 925µs mean). Wasm cert verify is only 90µs — much less than the cross-DO IPC overhead. The substrate's CPU cost is small; the storage round-trips are what to optimize if anyone needs more headroom.

**Sum-of-parts check**: step means total ~898µs vs full-pipeline mean 925µs — no hidden orchestrator overhead. Pipeline is the sum of its parts.

**Methodology gotcha**: workerd's `performance.now()` is 1ms-quantized (Spectre defense). Per-step rows are computed by timing N=500 loops and dividing — gives ~5µs resolution. Full-pipeline p50/p99 are 1ms-granular but the distribution surfaces tail behavior.

**NOT closing**. The bead lists 5 surfaces; this session covered lease-middleware only. Sub-bead `cloister-e4daae` filed for the remaining four:
- Tools/call dispatch overhead (pre-auth vs post-auth gate)
- Isolated TrustStore RPC under load
- Disclosure endpoint throughput
- Cold-start cluster boot

Caveat in the writeup: numbers are local workerd, not CF prod. Different shape expected on CF edge.

title: Prompt-injection vs vault-slice failure-mode demo
description:
Surfaced 2026-05-10 from outside review:

> "Demo of the prompt-injection-vs-vault-slice failure mode — still want this."

ADR-0010 (vault + bundle clusters) defines slice tokens as the capability primitive: a bundle gets a token scoped to a specific slice of vault (e.g. `slice:github-creds`), not the unrestricted vault. The security claim: even if a bundle is fully compromised (prompt-injected into running attacker code), it can only exfil what its slice grants — not the whole vault.

The reviewer wants this CLAIM demonstrated with a working failure mode: a deliberately-vulnerable test bundle that gets prompt-injected, attempts to access vault entries outside its slice, and gets denied at the substrate layer.

## What to build

A `test/security/prompt-injection.test.ts` (or similar) that:

1. **Sets up a slice token** for a hypothetical bundle scoped to a narrow slice (e.g. `slice:test-app-config`).
2. **Simulates a compromised bundle** that tries to read OUTSIDE its slice (`slice:github-pat`, `slice:master-key`, etc.).
3. **Asserts** the unauthorized reads fail at the substrate (vault layer), NOT at the application layer. The compromised bundle can do anything it wants in JS — the substrate is the gate.

The "prompt injection" framing is the threat model: a JS bundle has full control of its own heap + code. Even an attacker-controlled bundle can only reach what the slice token permits.

## What ships alongside

- README cross-link to the demo
- ADR-0010 amendment with the demo's findings
- Maybe a short blog-post-shaped doc explaining the model with the demo as the worked example (good OSS launch material)

## Depends on

This bead needs ADR-0010 implementation to land first. ADR-0010 is still Proposed (no vault DO + slice-token primitive in the codebase yet). So this bead is a follow-up to whatever ADR-0010 implementation bead lands.

## Why this matters

The substrate's value proposition for OSS-launch is: "your AI tools are now capability-gated; even a hijacked tool can't escape its slice." Without a working demo, that claim is aspirational. With one, it's a property a reviewer can run themselves.

## Refs

- ADR-0010 (vault + bundle clusters) — defines slice tokens
- ADR-0011 (hypervisor/bundle boundary) — defines what "boundary" means
- threat-model.md §10 (substrate analysis) — already touches this but doesn't demonstrate

comments.text:
ADR-0013 landed (b22c320). This unblocks the demo by ratifying the enforcement model so the demo has something concrete to demo against.

**What ADR-0013 settled:**

1. Vault is already lifted into cloister/vault/ — envelope encryption, allowedSubs glob lists, plaintext-stays-in-DO proxying, adversarial test corpus. No reinvention.
2. notme/docs/design/009 already specified the substrate enforcement model: V8 isolate boundary + service-binding-as-only-exit + no globalOutbound on the compromised isolate. cloister adopts this model verbatim.
3. **No new cryptographic envelope** for slice grants. The substrate IS the enforcement: a tool-bundle Worker either has the VAULT service binding or it doesn't; if it does, vault's allowedSubs decides which slices.
4. No Interlace-lease integration for in-cluster vault access. Lease certs are for the outside wire (per ADR-0005's 2026-04-30 amendment).

**Demo structure for this bead (now single-session):**

`test/security/prompt-injection.test.ts` runs against a workerd config with:
- `compromised-tool` Worker — identity `"bundle:test-app:malicious"`, has VAULT binding, no globalOutbound, no disk, no DO
- `trusted-tool` Worker — identity `"bundle:trusted-tool:probe"`, similar shape, different identity
- Vault with two credentials: one allowed for `bundle:test-app:*`, one allowed for `bundle:trusted-tool:*`

Assertions:
- compromised-tool reads its allowed credential → succeeds
- compromised-tool reads OUT-of-slice credential → 403 (credential bytes never reach its isolate)
- compromised-tool `fetch()` → `TypeError: fetch is not defined`
- compromised-tool tries to read vault Worker's KEK secret → `undefined` (different binding map)

Ready to build. Filing the demo work as a follow-up sub-bead since this bead has now been re-scoped (ADR-0013 sized it correctly).

| 0010 | **Proposed** | NO (vault + bundle clusters, no impl) | **Decide: status. ADR-0011 references it; cloister-74ce00 (prompt-injection demo) blocks on impl. Filing dependent bead doesn't move the ADR.** |

## Three concrete decisions

### ADR-0011 → Accepted

ADR-0011's three-criterion test (mediates / multi-bundle blast / singleton) is referenced by:
- ADR-0012's bolded justification for TrustStore being hypervisor-tier
- cloister-be0607's cluster.capnp `Bundle.tier` field (literally encodes the classification)
- threat-model.md's seam classification (hypervisor seams vs cluster seams)

It's load-bearing. Flip to Accepted with a 2026-05-10 amendment noting "consumed by cluster.capnp tier field; informed ADR-0012's split."

### ADR-0010 → stays Proposed (no implementation yet)

The vault-slice primitive isn't implemented. cloister-74ce00 (prompt-injection demo) depends on it. The honest status is Proposed; flipping prematurely would lose accountability.

Optional improvement: amend ADR-0010 with a 2026-05-10 note saying "still Proposed; implementation gated on a sub-bead (file when scoping begins)."

### ADR-0008 → keep Proposed OR mark Deferred

Companion-pool (ADR-0008) is about load-balancing across multiple cloister-companion sidecars. With ADR-0005's amendment (cloister ↔ companion is plain capnp IPC inside one trust boundary), the multi-companion case is less urgent. ADR-0009 Phase 1 (cluster-in-a-pod) puts companion as a sibling container, not a pool.

Recommend: mark Deferred with a note pointing at ADR-0009 Phase 1 + a "revisit when scale demands it" amendment. Don't reject — the design isn't wrong, just not currently needed.

title: Extract Interlace as a standalone spec + invite second implementor
description:
Surfaced 2026-05-10 from outside review:

> "A second Interlace implementor — the threat model strengthens the case for specifying Interlace as a standard, because the §13.2 'silence is evidence' claim now has a real-world falsification path that another implementer could test against."

Today cloister is the only Interlace implementation. §13.2's "silence is evidence" is a cryptographic invariant: every authenticated request writes a `peer_lease_counters` row (counter chain); a missing row in the disclosure stream is evidence the request was admitted off-record. The threat model now documents the chain mechanics precisely. **A second implementation would either:**

- Reach the same chain at the same hash for the same inputs (the invariant is confirmed across implementations), OR
- Diverge from cloister's chain (the invariant is falsified; one of the two implementations is wrong)

Without a second implementation, the claim is a unilateral assertion. With one, it's a property a third party can run independently.

## What "extract a spec" means

Pull the Interlace pieces out of cloister's ADRs + threat model into a vendor-neutral document. The pieces:

| Piece | Where it lives in cloister today | What the spec says |
|---|---|---|
| Lease envelope | ADR-0007 + lease-middleware.ts | header format, canonical bytes, sig algorithm |
| Cert format | cert_chain.rs + lease-middleware.ts | Interlace OID arc, claims layout |
| Chain hash | peer-lease-counters.ts | `sha256(prev_chain_hash \|\| cert_fp \|\| nonce \|\| ts)` |
| Bundle format | bundle-canonical.ts | RFC 8949 deterministic CBOR canonical bytes |
| Attestation chain | peer-attestations.ts | per-peer chain with prev_self_ref + prev_peer_ref |
| Disclosure endpoint | disclosure.ts + bdef0c | JSONL shape, cursor signing, constant-time error |
| §13.2 invariant | threat-model.md | "silence is evidence" — missing row proves admission off-record |

Extract these into:
- `interlace-spec/0.1.0/README.md` — the spec
- `interlace-spec/0.1.0/test-vectors/` — canonical inputs + expected hashes (lifted from cloister's gen-fixture.rs)
- `interlace-spec/0.1.0/wire/*.capnp` — schema definitions

The spec repo could be:
- A standalone GitHub repo (`agentic-research/interlace-spec`)
- Or `docs/interlace-spec/` inside cloister with a separate publishing path

## What "second implementor" means

A minimum-viable second implementation that:
1. Mints a cert against a test master
2. Signs canonical-bytes-for-a-test-request
3. Computes the chain hash
4. Reaches the same digest as cloister, on the same inputs

Could be:
- A Python reference impl (~200 LOC, just for cross-check)
- A Rust verifier (separate from cloister's wasm32 build)
- Even an external GitHub Action that runs the test vectors

The point isn't "another production-grade implementor" — it's "the spec is precise enough that two implementations reach the same bytes."

## Acceptance

- Spec docs extracted to `interlace-spec/0.1.0/`
- Test vectors generated from cloister's gen-fixture, checked in
- One alternate implementation passes the test vectors (Python preferred for "anyone can read it")
- README + ADR-0007 cross-link to the spec

## Out of scope

- Multi-vendor production deployments (too early)
- W3C / IETF standardization track (too heavy for now)
- Formal verification (too heavy)

## Refs

- threat-model.md §13.2 — the "silence is evidence" invariant this falsifies
- ADR-0007 (cloister) — Interlace substrate
- gen-fixture.rs (cloister) — canonical test vector source
- Outside review 2026-05-10

title: Drift prevention: single-source-of-truth for paths shared across apko / config.capnp / cluster.capnp
description:
Surfaced 2026-05-10 during cloister-be0607b (cluster-in-a-pod persistent volume work). The DO storage path is hard-coded in three files with no codegen relationship between them:

| File | What it says |
|---|---|
| `apko.yaml` | creates `/data` + `/data/do` directories at image build |
| `config.capnp` | `( path = "/data/do", writable = true )` for the do-storage service |
| `cluster.capnp` | `doStoragePath = "/var/lib/cloister/do"` (operator-facing) |

Drift is real: be0607a's cluster.capnp drift (introduced by me) was caught only because be0607b made me look at all three.

## Three options

A. **cluster.capnp is canonical**; emitters generate apko mkdir + workerd config from it. New emitters: `scripts/emit-apko.mjs` (path block) and `scripts/emit-workerd-config.mjs` (do-storage entry). cluster.capnp's `StoragePolicy.doStoragePath` becomes the source of truth.

B. **A shared `paths.capnp` (or paths.yaml) imported by all three** at build time. Smaller change but adds a 4th file; still needs codegen at apko + workerd-config layer.

C. **`task cluster:check` lints all three for agreement**. Reads each file, extracts the path, asserts equality. Convention-checked, not codegen'd. Smallest possible — ~50 lines of node script.

## Recommendation

**Start with C (lint), file A as a follow-up.** C catches drift in CI immediately; A is the right long-term answer once the path-coupling pattern shows up in more places (vault slice paths, UDS socket dirs, future manifest fields).

## Other paths likely to drift

Once the lint exists, audit for other coupled paths:
- UDS socket dir: `/run/cloister-uds/` (referenced in cluster.capnp Bundle.ipcSocket + emit-compose.mjs)
- Bundle entry-point paths: `src/bundles/<name>/index.ts` (would appear in cluster.capnp WorkerdBundle.entryPoint when those land)
- Vault paths under ADR-0010 (when implemented)

## Acceptance for the lint-only MVP

- `scripts/lint-paths.mjs` checks the three known paths agree
- `task cluster:check` invokes it; wired into `task lint`
- Mismatch produces a precise error message naming all three files

## Acceptance for the codegen path (follow-up)

- cluster.capnp `StoragePolicy` is the source
- `task cluster:emit` generates the path block in apko.yaml + the do-storage entry in config.capnp
- Removing the path from any consumer breaks the build (codegen requires it)

## Refs

- cloister-be0607a (just landed) — introduced cluster.capnp's `doStoragePath`
- cloister-be0607b — surfaced this drift question
- ADR-0004 — capnp manifest as the substrate

title: credential-isolation/v1: LLO publishes 10 conformance vectors, cloister runs zero
description:
LLO ships rs/ll-core/schema-spec/credential-isolation/v1/test-vectors/ — TEN vector files with SHA-256 pins in VECTORS.sha256, including adversarial ones: adversarial-credential-leak.json, adversarial-tamper-canonical.json, adversarial-malformed-envelope.json, injection-collision.json, reserved-response-headers.json, path-parsing.json, error-responses.json, proxy-envelope-canonical.json, receipt-commitment.json, injection-fixtures.json.

LLO's README states the conformance criterion outright: 'anyone building a second implementation... If you reach the same digests on the test vectors, you are conformant.'

Cloister IS that second implementation. src/routes/vault-proxy.ts is 770 lines implementing the wire contract, citing leyline-schema-spec/credential-isolation/v1/wire/{proxy-envelope,receipt-commitment,injection-strategies,error-responses}.md throughout. It has SEVEN test files (vault-proxy.test.ts alone is 1045 lines). None consume a single LLO vector — every assertion is hand-written against cloister's own reading of the spec.

## Why this is the ADR-0063 failure class, one contract over
lint:spec-citation verifies 36 citations RESOLVE — it proves cloister POINTS AT LLO's spec. Nothing proves cloister OBEYS it. That is precisely how PR #260 passed green: it cited the right contract and implemented a different one.

Stakes are higher here than execution/v1. This is the credential surface, and the unrun vectors include the adversarial credential-leak and tamper cases — exactly the properties the capability exists to guarantee.

## NOT a claim that vault-proxy is wrong
The hand-written tests are extensive and probably assert the right behaviours. The gap is that they assert them against cloister's READING, not against the spec's published digests. Divergence would be silent.

## The fix is a worked shape
scripts/test/llo-execution-vector.test.mjs (c5cfee9) is the pattern for execution/v1: vendor byte-for-byte under the upstream digest into test/fixtures/, assert the digest, then drive the PRODUCTION path. Cloister CI has no LLO checkout — that is why vendoring-under-digest beats reading a checkout (same reason rs/crates/cas/tests/confinement_digest.rs inlines confinement/v1's manifest). Ten vectors wants a small harness iterating the VECTORS.sha256 manifest, not ten hand-written tests.

## Conformance status, four shared contracts
- confinement/v1          — conformant (rs/crates/cas/tests/confinement_digest.rs)
- execution/v1            — conformant as of c5cfee9
- credential-isolation/v1 — CITED, NOT CONFORMED (this bead)
- mcp-tool/v1             — cited, not conformed (separate, much smaller)

rosary/schemas/cloister.capnp is a verbatim vendored copy of LLO's rs/ll-core/schema-capnp/schemas/net.capnp (fileId @0xa25bb2a310446125, LLO commit 78638f3, PR #225 / ley-line-open-083344), with exactly two documented deltas (filename kept for capnpc module naming; Go annotations stripped) and a header that says 'do NOT hand-edit the frame structs here.'

And it runs the vectors: schemas/leyline-net/v1/test-vectors/ drives src/leyline_net_vectors.rs as the drift gate, bead rosary-086973.

So the exact discipline this bead asks for — vendor the upstream schema under a documented pin, then gate on the upstream's own conformance vectors — is already shipped in a sibling repo against a different LLO contract. This is not a new practice to invent or justify; it is one cloister has not adopted for credential-isolation/v1.

Worth citing in the implementation: rosary's header comment is a good model for what test/fixtures/llo-execution-v1/README.md should say for each vendored contract.

title: The vault has no production write path — DEV_VAULT_SEED is the only way a credential gets in
description:
Filed 2026-07-28. Operator instinct: the dev path "may end up working" while the
real mechanism goes unbuilt. It is worse than that — the real mechanism does not
exist.

## Evidence

    vaultSlice            0 occurrences in cluster.toml, manifest/cluster.capnp,
                          src/manifest/cluster-types.ts — no schema field, no
                          declarations
    putCredential         exactly ONE caller: vault-store.ts:470, inside
                          #devSeed, gated on CLOISTER_MODE === "dev"
    /vault/proxy          the only vault route — read + inject side

`src/vault-store.ts:451` states the design intent plainly: the dev seed ingests
"in-boundary, **no external write route**".

So the vault today has a working READ path and NO production WRITE path. The
only way a credential enters is `DEV_VAULT_SEED`, which requires
`CLOISTER_MODE=dev`.

## Why this is not merely incomplete

ADR-0010 makes vault slices the binding substrate, and CLAUDE.md's "What NOT to
add" forbids env-var bindings for new credentials on that basis — new bindings
"should land as `vaultSlice` declarations on a bundle". That instruction cannot
currently be followed: there is nothing to declare into.

The failure mode is the one this substrate keeps producing. `task harness:dev`
works. Credentials flow. The vault proxy injects. Everything LOOKS like the
vault is in use — and every part of it is a dev seam that `lint:no-dev-mode`
exists to keep out of committed config. The path that ships and the path that
is exercised are disjoint, and the working one is the one that must not ship.

Note the "no external write route" decision is GOOD and should survive: an
externally-reachable credential-write endpoint is an attack surface worth not
having. The gap is that no alternative was built alongside it.

## The question to answer

How does a credential reach the vault in production, given no external write
route? Candidates, none decided:

1. **Sealed at deploy time** — KEK-wrapped material provisioned with the bundle,
   decrypted in-boundary by the per-bundle vault DO (ADR-0021) using the KEK
   from the declared source (ADR-0014: Keychain / libsecret / file / env).
2. **Operator CLI writing DO storage directly** — same trust boundary as the
   dev seed, no network surface, but needs a story for a remote/CF deployment
   where the operator has no local DO.
3. **Slice declaration resolved at build** — `vaultSlice` on a bundle names the
   credential; the value arrives by (1). This is what ADR-0010 implies and what
   CLAUDE.md instructs people to write, so it probably wants to exist regardless
   of which mechanism backs it.

Blocking question for whoever picks this up: which of these does a Cloudflare
deployment support, given the operator cannot reach the DO's storage directly?
That constraint likely decides it.

## Relation to the harness

cloister-742e19 shipped harness targets whose credential path is the vault. In
custody mode the key is written to DEV_VAULT_SEED — so the harness feature is
currently only operable in dev mode. That is not a defect in 742e19; it is this
gap surfacing through it.

title: Derive MCP tool inputSchemaJson from TS handler types instead of hand-written inline JSON
description:
Surfaced 2026-05-10. cloister.capnp embeds JSON Schema strings inline as `inputSchemaJson` capnp Text fields:

```capnp
( name        = "bead_create",
  description = "Create a new bead (work item) in the store for the given repo.",
  inputSchemaJson = "{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"repo\":{\"type\":\"string\"},...,\"required\":[\"repo\",\"title\"]}"
),
```

Eleven such fields today (bead_*, lsp_*). Three problems:

1. **Hard to read/edit** — escaped quotes inside a capnp Text inside a manifest. Editors don't help; can't lint the JSON itself easily.
2. **No compile-time coupling to handlers** — the `bead_create` handler in TS accepts an args object; nothing checks that the manifest's inputSchemaJson matches the handler's actual accepted shape.
3. **Drift risk** — if a handler adds a parameter, the JSON Schema must be hand-updated. Forgetting = MCP clients see a stale schema; they pass the new field, the handler ignores or rejects it.

## What MCP actually requires on the wire

MCP `tools/list` returns each tool's `inputSchema` as JSON Schema. Clients consume this to validate args before sending. So the WIRE format is JSON Schema; that doesn't change.

What CAN change: how the schema is **authored**. Today: hand-written inline. Tomorrow: derived from a typed handler signature.

## Three options

### A. Derive from zod (or @sinclair/typebox) schemas in the handler module

```ts
// src/backends/beads.ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { zodToJsonSchema } from "zod-to-json-schema";

export const beadCreateArgs = z.object({
  repo:     z.string(),
  title:    z.string(),
  description: z.string().optional(),
  priority: z.number().int().min(0).max(4).optional(),
  labels:   z.array(z.string()).optional(),
  created_by: z.string().optional(),
}).strict();

export async function beadCreate(env: Env, args: z.infer<typeof beadCreateArgs>) {
  // handler implementation; args is fully typed
}
```

Then a build step extracts schemas from the handler modules, emits them into cloister.capnp's `inputSchemaJson` field at codegen time. The TS handler is the source of truth.

**Pros:**
- One source of truth (the zod schema)
- Handlers are typed end-to-end (no `as Record<string, unknown>` casts)
- Validation happens at the handler boundary automatically (zod throws on mismatch)
- JSON Schema generation is well-trodden (zod-to-json-schema is mature)

**Cons:**
- Requires zod (~30KB minified) added to the cluster
- Bigger refactor: every backend module declares its schemas
- The manifest becomes "derived from handlers" instead of "drives handlers" in this dimension; might confuse some readers

### B. External JSON Schema files referenced by path

```capnp
inputSchemaPath = "tools/bead_create.schema.json"
```

**Pros:**
- Editable as JSON (with editor JSON support)
- No new TS dep

**Cons:**
- Still no type-coupling to handlers (drift still possible)
- More files to manage
- Not a real fix for the underlying drift problem

### C. Capnp struct schemas with a JSON-Schema emitter

Define each tool's input shape as a capnp struct in a tools-spec.capnp file. Emit JSON Schema from capnp's introspection at build.

**Pros:**
- Fully typed in capnp
- Single source of truth in capnp's schema language

**Cons:**
- Capnp doesn't natively express JSON Schema's full surface (regex patterns, descriptions on individual fields, oneOf, conditionals). Would need to extend with annotations.
- Awkward for tool authors (they're writing capnp instead of TS)

## Recommendation: Option A (zod-derived)

It's the architecturally honest answer. The TS handler is where args are USED; the schema describing args should live next to that code, not in a separate manifest field that a human has to manually keep in sync.

## Migration path

1. Add zod as a dep (also useful for request body validation in many places)
2. Pick ONE backend (e.g. BeadStore — simplest schema surface) to migrate
3. Build script extracts the zod schema → JSON Schema → injects into the generated manifest TS module (alongside the existing inline strings, not yet replacing them)
4. Add a lint that asserts the generated schema matches the inline string
5. Once parity is proven for all backends, drop the inline `inputSchemaJson` field entirely; the manifest reads schemas from the handler-side codegen

Migration is ~6 sub-beads; not in-this-session work.

## Out of scope

- JSON Schema → TypeScript type generation (the OTHER direction; we're going TS → JSON Schema, which is well-supported)
- Runtime validation of handler args (zod gives this for free; could be a separate sub-bead about turning it on)
- Tool-aware ADR (whether tool definitions belong in cloister.capnp at all, or in a separate tools.capnp)

## Refs

- ADR-0006 — derived tool schemas (this is the OTHER kind of derived schema; that ADR is about MCP tool schemas pulled from upstream services like mache. The proposal here is about COMPILE-TIME schemas for cloister-resident tools.)
- cloister.capnp lines 75-150 (the inline `inputSchemaJson` fields)
- src/backends/durable-object.ts (handler dispatch — would benefit from typed args)

comments.text:
Full migration landed (fe3aad2).

**Source of truth: src/tool-schemas/** (zod, 14 tools across 3 groups). Wire pipeline:

```
src/tool-schemas/*.ts  →  z.toJSONSchema()  →  src/generated/tool-schemas.ts
                                                       │ (overlay)
cloister.capnp  →  build-manifest.mjs  ←──────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
                 src/generated/manifest.ts  (Gateway w/ injected schemas)
```

**Drift defenses:**
1. **Build-time**: `build-manifest.mjs` overlays zod-derived schemas onto manifest tools by name. If a tool carries a non-empty inline `inputSchemaJson` that disagrees with the zod source, the build fails with a structural diff.
2. **Test-time**: `test/manifest/tool-schemas.test.ts` (3 cases) enforces: every manifest tool has a zod schema; every zod schema is wired to a manifest tool; every generated `inputSchemaJson` is a parseable JSON Schema object. All pass.
3. **Type-level**: `z.infer<typeof X>` is the handler args type — drift becomes a TS error rather than a silent wire mismatch.

**Wire format changes**:
- `priority`: `enum:[0,1,2,3,4]` → `{minimum:0,maximum:4}`. Semantically identical (any integer in 0-4 passes), simpler shape for clients to render as a numeric input.
- All bead/lsp/lifecycle tool schemas now ship `additionalProperties:false`. Typo'd arg names get a validator error at the wire instead of silent handler ignore — closes the original "schemas could disagree with handlers" hazard at the source.

**Deps**: `zod ^4.4.3`, `tsx ^4.21.0` (build-only). Removed `zod-to-json-schema` — it's a v3-era helper that emits empty `{}` against zod v4's revamped `_def` shape; zod v4's native `z.toJSONSchema()` replaces it.

590/590 tests pass. All lints (paths, timing, mermaid, parity) green.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

title: Drift prevention class 2: timing/security constants coupled across repos (cert TTL ↔ bundle refresh ↔ alarm cadence ↔ seen_nonces eviction)
description:
Surfaced 2026-05-10 right after `cloister-7c12cc` (path drift). The user flagged that path drift is annoying; **timing-constant drift is silently insecure**.

> "the same is true for say the 300s timeout that depends on the DO alarm. if either are wrong it's evil"

This bead is the SAME shape as 7c12cc (drift prevention), but for security-affecting magic numbers. Different invariant style, different cost-of-drift profile (security, not just operational).

## The coupled timing constants today

| Constant | Where it lives | Coupled to | Invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cert TTL | notme/worker (cert mint), 300s | cloister's clock-skew bound, validity window | clock-skew (60s) << cert TTL (300s); else clock-skew approaches the cert window and replay-by-time is possible |
| Bundle max age | notme/worker `BUNDLE_MAX_AGE_MS` (5 min) | cloister's `BUNDLE_REFRESH_MS` (4 min) | cloister.refresh < notme.max_age; else cloister fetches a stale bundle that notme already considers revoked |
| seen_nonces eviction | cloister `pruneSeenNoncesBefore` (currently no schedule) | cert TTL | eviction window >= cert TTL; else nonces are pruned before the cert that minted them expires, replays slip through |
| Pending attestations DO alarm | cloister-be0607c retry pump (not yet impl) | retry backoff schedule (`RETRY_BACKOFF_MS = [30s, 1m, 2m, 5m, 10m]`) | alarm cadence MUST NOT fire faster than the backoff says; else exponential pressure on TrustStore |
| Disclosure cursor TTL | cloister `signCursor` (currently unbounded) | cert TTL | cursor age check, if any, should be at least cert TTL so legitimate paginators don't get rejected mid-page |

## Why this is "evil"

Path drift = container fails to start, operator sees the error in logs.

Timing drift = the cluster RUNS, but with a security property silently violated:
- Replays accepted that shouldn't be
- Stale bundles trusted that shouldn't be
- Nonces evicted before they should be

Most cases produce no log output. The only signal is from §13.2's "silence is evidence" disclosure — and even that requires a peer noticing.

## The relationships, written down

```
notme.cert_ttl_secs (300) >= cloister.MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS / 1000 (60)
  + safety_margin (≥ 4×; 300 / 60 = 5×, ok today)

notme.BUNDLE_MAX_AGE_MS (300_000) > cloister.BUNDLE_REFRESH_MS (240_000)
  + safety_margin (60s today; ok)

cloister.seen_nonces_eviction_window >= notme.cert_ttl_secs
  (eviction NOT YET implemented; prune-on-schedule + window must >= 300s)

cloister.pending_attestations_alarm_cadence >=
  min(cloister.RETRY_BACKOFF_MS) (30_000)
  (alarm not yet wired; when be0607c lands)

cloister.disclosure_cursor_age_max >= notme.cert_ttl_secs
  (paginators using a cert MUST be able to finish before the cert
   expires; cursor age MUST allow that)
```

## Three options

### A. Cross-repo shared constants file (`interlace-constants.json`)

The Interlace spec extraction (cloister-765132) is the natural home. A canonical JSON like:
```json
{
  "cert_ttl_secs": 300,
  "bundle_max_age_secs": 300,
  "bundle_refresh_secs": 240,
  "max_clock_skew_secs": 60,
  "seen_nonces_eviction_secs": 360,
  "min_retry_backoff_secs": 30
}
```

Both notme and cloister read this at build (codegen → constants module). The relationships are also declared as invariants:
```json
"invariants": [
  "bundle_refresh_secs < bundle_max_age_secs",
  "seen_nonces_eviction_secs >= cert_ttl_secs",
  "max_clock_skew_secs * 4 <= cert_ttl_secs"
]
```

Build-time check enforces invariants.

**Pros:** True source of truth across repos. Spec-shaped (matches cloister-765132 direction).
**Cons:** Cross-repo coupling becomes explicit (good in principle, more PRs in practice).

### B. Lint that knows the relationships, no shared constants

`scripts/lint-timing-invariants.mjs` reads each repo's constants from where they live, asserts the invariants. Wired into `task lint` + a CI workflow that pulls notme as a sibling checkout.

**Pros:** No cross-repo dep needed today. Lower upfront cost.
**Cons:** Two sources of truth, lint is the only check, lint can lag behind real changes.

### C. Document only, no automated check

Write the invariants in the threat model + ADR-0007 amendment. Operator/reviewer enforces.

**Pros:** Zero cost.
**Cons:** Human enforcement = drift returns. Useless for OSS where multiple operators may not have the context.

## Recommendation

**B for now, A as part of cloister-765132 (Interlace spec extraction).**

B is small and immediate; A is right when the spec exists.

## Acceptance for B (lint only)

- `scripts/lint-timing-invariants.mjs` reads:
  - `notme/worker/src/revocation.ts` for `BUNDLE_MAX_AGE_MS`
  - `notme/worker/src/cert-authority.ts` for cert TTL
  - `cloister/src/storage/ca-bundle-cache.ts` for `BUNDLE_REFRESH_MS`
  - `cloister/src/routes/lease-middleware.ts` for `MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS`
  - `cloister/src/storage/seen-nonces.ts` (when eviction lands) for the window
  - `cloister/src/storage/pending-attestations.ts` for `RETRY_BACKOFF_MS`
- Each invariant in the table above asserted; mismatch produces a precise error
- Wired into `task lint`
- CI pulls notme as a sibling checkout (or a pinned commit) so the lint can run

## Acceptance for A (cross-repo shared constants, follow-up)

- `interlace-spec/0.1.0/constants.json` (under cloister-765132)
- Both notme and cloister codegen TS/Go constants modules from it
- Invariants declared; build fails on violation

## Refs

- cloister-7c12cc — sibling bead for path drift (this is the timing-class equivalent)
- cloister-765132 — Interlace spec extraction (where the cross-repo source-of-truth would live)
- threat-model.md §6.2.7 (clock-skew), §5.2 (bundle staleness), §6.2.3 (replay defense) — all touch timing invariants
- ADR-0007 audit amendment 2026-05-08 — documented the BUNDLE_MAX_AGE_MS relationship
